items.note: self-assigned authority label; nobody with actual authority calls their work this
items.example: Our thought leadership content positions us as industry experts.

items.note: double jargon stack; combines two of the most overloaded corporate verbs
items.example: We need to leverage synergies across business units to drive growth.

items.note: catch-all phrase for any technology adoption; almost never means anything specific
items.example: Our digital transformation initiative will modernize operations enterprise-wide.

items.note: military metaphor applied to any important task; inflates routine priorities
items.example: Completing the migration on time is mission critical to our Q3 goals.

items.note: euphemism for layoffs; corporate speak to avoid naming what is actually happening
items.example: The company announced a rightsizing effort affecting 12% of the workforce.

items.note: financial metaphor applied to any obstacle; widely overused in earnings calls and business writing
items.example: We face significant headwinds in the current macroeconomic environment.

items.note: companion to headwinds; applied to any favorable condition regardless of specificity
items.example: Strong consumer demand provides tailwinds for our growth trajectory.

items.note: self-congratulatory descriptor that adds no information; all planning is forward-facing
items.example: Forward-thinking companies are investing in AI to stay ahead of competitors.

items.note: significance inflation applied to incremental or routine improvements
items.example: This platform is revolutionizing the way teams collaborate and communicate.

items.note: product-pitch pivot formula; signals AI-generated marketing copy
items.example: Managing data at scale is hard. That's where we come in.

items.note: marketing promise that no product can keep; used to sell any software or service
items.example: Future-proof your infrastructure with our cloud-native platform.

items.note: self-positioning claim used by any company regardless of actual market position
items.example: We are at the forefront of sustainable packaging innovation.

items.note: performed excitement in press releases and LinkedIn posts; almost always AI or PR template
items.example: We are thrilled to announce our partnership with Acme Corporation.

items.note: performed enthusiasm opener for announcements; near-universal in AI-generated LinkedIn posts
items.example: Excited to share that we just closed our Series B funding round.

items.note: ironic cliche: using a cliche to describe the absence of cliches
items.example: Success in this role requires out-of-the-box thinking and creative problem-solving.

items.note: negotiation jargon applied to any arrangement; makes any deal sound mutually beneficial without analysis
items.example: The partnership creates a win-win situation for both organizations.

items.note: filler descriptor; any planned action is proactive by definition
items.example: We take a proactive approach to risk management and compliance.

items.note: applied to incremental changes; Kuhn's original meaning has been entirely diluted
items.example: Cloud computing represents a paradigm shift in how businesses manage IT.

items.note: MBA jargon for 'what we offer'; replaces a direct description with an abstract frame
items.example: Our core value proposition centers on speed, reliability, and ease of use.

items.note: management consulting term for 'what we're good at'; widely overused and emptied of meaning
items.example: We focus on our core competencies and outsource non-strategic functions.

items.note: legitimate phrase but overused as a filler assertion; FP risk high in technical/process writing
items.example: We follow industry best practices for data security and governance.

items.note: vague growth phrase that avoids specifying what will change or by how much
items.example: The funding will allow us to scale our operations across new markets.

items.note: technical term used as a metaphor for human capacity; FP risk high in technical contexts
items.example: I don't have the bandwidth to take on another project this quarter.

items.note: Christensen's specific term applied to any product launch; almost always misused
items.example: Our disruptive innovation is challenging the established players in the market.

items.note: doubles two overloaded AI adjectives/nouns; describes any product network with vague grandeur
items.example: We have built a robust ecosystem of integrations and technology partners.

items.note: near-universal marketing phrase for any software connection; no integration is actually seamless
items.example: Our platform offers seamless integration with your existing tools.

items.note: scope inflation claiming completeness; rarely accompanied by specifics
items.example: We provide an end-to-end solution for supply chain management.

items.note: overused in both AI writing and business communication as a substitute for 'detailed analysis'
items.example: Let's schedule a deep dive into the Q4 performance metrics.

items.note: meeting-speak for 'follow up'; the solo form without 'around' is equally sloppy
items.example: Let's circle back on this after we hear from the legal team.

items.note: process platitude substituting for a description of actual coordination mechanisms
items.example: The weekly standup helps us keep all stakeholders aligned on priorities.

items.note: noun-phrase jargon for 'teams agreeing'; abstracts away the actual work of coordination
items.example: Cross-functional alignment is essential before we kick off the initiative.

items.note: management jargon for 'getting people to agree'; widely used in any organizational context
items.example: We need stakeholder buy-in before the project can move forward.

items.note: startup/marketing frame applied to any plan to sell something; often filler in pitch decks
items.example: Our go-to-market strategy focuses on enterprise sales and channel partners.

items.note: startup jargon that has spread into general business writing; often used without its precise meaning
items.example: We are still iterating on the product to achieve product-market fit.

items.note: self-labeling; the takeaways should be evident without announcement
items.example: Here are the key takeaways from today's leadership summit.

items.note: financial term misused as a filler phrase meaning 'in summary' or 'bottom line'
items.example: Net net, we need to cut costs by 15% to hit our EBITDA targets.

items.text: at the end of the day
items.note: spoken-word filler phrase signaling a false 'bottom line' conclusion; appears in research at 12x AI frequency
items.example: At the end of the day, what matters is customer satisfaction.

items.note: vague adjective meaning 'having impact'; widely flagged as non-standard and overused in corporate writing
items.example: We are looking for candidates who want to do impactful work at scale.

items.note: corporate nouning of 'learn'; 'lessons' or 'findings' is always clearer
items.example: We will share the key learnings from the pilot program with the broader team.

items.note: corporate jargon for 'brainstorming'; adds syllables without adding meaning
items.example: We will hold an ideation session to generate concepts for the rebranding.

items.note: legitimate acronym in business contexts but overused as a vague filler; FP risk high in actual analytics writing
items.example: We need to define the KPIs that will measure the success of this initiative.

items.note: signals 'we considered everything' without describing what was considered
items.example: We take a holistic approach to employee wellness and development.

items.note: appears 18x more often in AI text; 'engagement' as a vague metric substituting for a real description
items.example: Our content strategy is designed to drive engagement across all channels.

items.note: appears 20x more often in AI text; pairs two overused corporate terms into a hollow directive
items.example: We create an environment that fosters innovation and creative thinking.

items.note: all decisions should be informed by data; phrase signals that you value data without saying how
items.example: Our culture of data-driven decisions separates us from the competition.

items.note: vague efficiency claim with no specification of which processes or by how much
items.example: Automation helps us streamline processes and reduce operational overhead.

items.note: self-description that says nothing; all professionals claim to be results-driven
items.example: We are a results-driven organization focused on delivering measurable outcomes.

items.note: management jargon for 'everyone agreeing on direction'; vague without context
items.example: Strategic alignment across departments is critical to executing our vision.

items.note: legitimate software development term but widely misapplied as a generic flexibility claim
items.example: We use agile methodology to adapt quickly to changing market conditions.

items.note: startup jargon for changing direction; overused to describe any strategy change, however minor
items.example: The company had to pivot its business model in response to market feedback.

items.note: stacks two overused corporate words; claims a full sales or product backlog with no evidence
items.example: We enter Q4 with a robust pipeline of enterprise deals close to signing.

items.note: spelled-out form of KPIs used when writers want to sound thorough; typically filler in summaries
items.example: We track key performance indicators to monitor progress toward our goals.

items.note: hollow superlative applied to any above-average effort; cliche in HR and marketing writing
items.example: Our team consistently goes above and beyond to deliver exceptional results.

items.text: move at the speed of business
items.note: filler phrase implying urgency without specifying what 'speed' means or how it is achieved
items.example: Modern IT infrastructure must move at the speed of business to remain competitive.

items.note: nearly identical to the existing 'drive value'; a second variant of the same hollow promise
items.example: Every feature we ship is designed to deliver value to our enterprise customers.

items.note: agricultural metaphor applied to any interdepartmental collaboration; sounds creative while saying nothing
items.example: We encourage cross-pollination of ideas between our engineering and design teams.

items.note: HR jargon for recruiting prospects; 'pipeline' applied to people dehumanizes them into a process metaphor
items.example: Partnerships with universities help us build a strong talent pipeline.

items.note: self-applied credential that no actual authority ever uses to describe themselves
items.example: He is recognized as a thought leader in the field of sustainable finance.

items.note: marketing jargon for writing about a company; frames advertising as narrative art
items.example: Effective brand storytelling builds emotional connections with your audience.

items.note: sales jargon for customer problems; overused in AI-generated marketing and product writing
items.example: Our product addresses the core pain points of enterprise procurement teams.

items.note: cliche empowerment metaphor applied to any autonomous role or decision-making context
items.example: Our platform puts customers in the driver's seat of their own data.

items.note: appears 13x more often in AI text; generic agency verb applied to any product or initiative
items.example: We empower organizations to make faster, smarter decisions.

items.note: appears 15x more often in AI text; vague promise formula applied to any capability
items.example: Our platform helps businesses unlock the potential of their data.

items.note: appears 17x more often in AI text; metaphor applied to any technology or capability
items.example: Organizations can harness the power of AI to transform customer service.

items.note: appears 16x more often in AI text; signals complexity without describing it
items.example: We help businesses navigate the complexities of regulatory compliance.

items.note: marketing superlative applied to any current technology; often means nothing more than 'recent'
items.example: Our state-of-the-art platform leverages the latest advances in machine learning.

items.note: vague subject that avoids naming the actual people involved in a decision
items.example: We will present the proposal to key stakeholders before the end of the quarter.

items.note: used to claim universality without specifying scope; classic hedge-by-expansion phrase
items.example: Performance improvements were seen across the board following the platform upgrade.

items.note: game theory term misapplied in corporate writing to describe any competitive situation
items.example: We don't see this as a zero-sum competition; there is room for multiple players.

items.note: military jargon for a special task force; applied to any project team in corporate contexts
items.example: We assembled a tiger team to address the critical infrastructure issue.

items.note: tech industry phrase for using your own product; now widely applied as a proof-of-confidence claim
items.example: We eat our own dog food, running our entire infrastructure on our platform.

items.note: startup hyperbole for any significant growth target; rarely based on a specific plan
items.example: Our goal is to achieve 10x growth in ARR over the next three years.

items.note: informal hyperbole for any positive performance; canonical in tech startup culture and LinkedIn posts
items.example: The sales team is absolutely crushing it this quarter.

items.note: phrase for testing an idea without committing to it; classic corporate hedging idiom
items.example: Let's run it up the flagpole and see if leadership has any concerns.

items.note: noun and adjective form overused to describe any beneficial contribution
items.example: The consulting engagement delivered clear value-add beyond the initial scope.

items.note: corporate euphemism for sharing confidential information; widely criticized and still in use
items.example: They were willing to open the kimono and share detailed financials during due diligence.

items.note: idiom for being prepared or organized; overused in meeting and email contexts
items.example: We need to get all our ducks in a row before the investor presentation.

items.note: phrase that claims to simplify something without actually doing so
items.example: It all boils down to execution; the strategy is already strong.

items.note: altitude metaphor for high-level summary; pairs with 'drill-down' to structure any presentation
items.example: Let me give you a 30,000-foot view before we get into the details.

items.note: marketing superlative applied to any product without defining the industry or the metrics of leadership
items.example: We offer industry-leading response times and customer satisfaction scores.
